kinds.d: Loose cut red corundum, or ruby cutting rough.

x.d: Ruby from the Mogok Valley, Myanmar, for centuries the main source; the brightest red is called pigeon's blood and commands a large premium.

v.d: 23.1 carats, mined in Mogok, National Museum of Natural History

x.dt: pigeon's blood red · usually heated · few fine stones found recently

x.d: Ruby historically mined in Thailand and in the Pailin and Samlout areas of Cambodia.
Ruby from the northeastern Montepuez mine, found in 2009 and soon the world's most productive source of gem ruby.
x.dt: large supply · heat and glass-filling treatments common

x.d: Ruby cut as a cabochon to show a three- or six-ray star from oriented rutile silk.
x.dt: cabochon · asterism best seen under a single light

kinds.d: Loose cut corundum of any colour but red, or sapphire cutting rough.

x.d: Cornflower-blue sapphire from the Paddar Valley in the Jammu region of India, mined mainly in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

v.d: Set for Kashmir stones in 2014 and 2015

x.d: Sapphire from Sri Lanka, mostly from the Ratnapura area, source of many famous stars.

v.d: 563.4 carats, American Museum of Natural History

x.d: Pink-orange to orange-pink sapphire, first found in Sri Lanka; the name comes from a Sanskrit word for lotus colour.
Cornflower-blue sapphire from Yogo Gulch near Lewistown, Montana, typically sold untreated.
x.dt: small stones · large faceted stones rare

x.d: Sapphire in yellow, orange, green, brown, purple or showing two or more colours; Australia is the largest source of parti stones.
Sapphire cut as a cabochon to show a six-ray star from rutile needles.

v.d: 3,536-carat purple star sapphire from near Ratnapura

x.d: Sapphire blue in daylight and purple under incandescent light; sources include Madagascar, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Tanzania.

kinds.d: Loose cut green beryl, or emerald cutting rough.

x.d: Emerald from Muzo, Coscuez and Chivor, historically the largest producer and prized for intense green.
Emerald from the Kafubu River area; Zambia is the second-largest producer, with better transparency than most Colombian stones.
Rare Colombian emerald with ray-like spokes of dark impurities.
Emerald from Bahia and other Brazilian localities.

kinds.d: Cut beryl other than emerald: aquamarine, morganite, heliodor, goshenite and red beryl.

x.d: Blue to cyan beryl coloured by iron, found in Sri Lanka, Brazil, Pakistan, Mount Antero (Colorado) and many other places.

v.d: Deep blue beryl whose colour fades with light or heat

x.dt: pale blue to cyan · often heated

x.d: Pink beryl, light pink to rose, coloured by manganese; sometimes heated to remove yellow patches.
x.dt: pink to rose · colour banding common

x.d: Golden-yellow to greenish-yellow beryl coloured by iron.
Very rare red beryl first described in 1904 from Utah's Thomas Range, usually highly included.
x.dt: Utah and New Mexico · usually small and included

x.d: Colourless beryl named for Goshen, Massachusetts; historically used in lenses and spectacles.

kinds.d: Loose cut spinel, or spinel cutting rough.

x.d: Spinel in red and pink, coloured by chromium, long found at Mogok and in Badakhshan.

v.d: Spinel in the British Crown Jewels
Spinel in the British Crown Jewels

x.d: Spinel from marbles at Mahenge, Tanzania; glowing pink and blue stones found there since 2000.
Pure blue spinel coloured by small amounts of cobalt.

kinds.d: Cut chrysoberyl: colour-change alexandrite, cat's-eye cymophane and plain yellow-green stones.

x.d: Chrysoberyl that looks green in daylight and red under incandescent light, first from the Urals; larger stones now come from Brazil.
x.dt: colour change from chromium · beware 'simulated alexandrite' corundum or spinel

x.d: Translucent yellowish chrysoberyl with a chatoyant band from rutile inclusions; only chrysoberyl may be called cat's eye unqualified.

kinds.d: Loose cut blue-violet zoisite, or tanzanite cutting rough.

x.d: Blue-violet zoisite from a small mining area near the Merelani Hills, Tanzania, the only source; found in 1967 and introduced by Tiffany & Co. in 1968.
x.dt: brownish rough heated to blue-violet · trichroic unheated, dichroic after heating · no universal grading standard

kinds.d: Loose faceted or cabochon tourmaline, or facet-grade tourmaline rough sold by weight. Uncut specimens are under Tourmaline in Minerals & crystals.

x.d: Copper-bearing elbaite with intense blue-green colour, from Rio Grande do Norte in Brazil, later Nigeria and Mozambique.

v.d: Paler and less saturated than Brazilian material
More recent source with intense stones

x.dt: small stones · neon blue to green

x.d: Red or pinkish-red elbaite.
Rare rich green dravite from Tanzania coloured by chromium.
Indicolite is light blue to bluish-green elbaite; verdelite is green elbaite.
Bicolour tourmaline green at one end and pink at the other, or green outside and pink inside.
Sodium-magnesium brown tourmaline, named by Tschermak in 1884 from Dobrova near Dravograd.

kinds.d: Loose faceted or cabochon garnet of any species, or garnet cutting rough. Uncut specimens are under Garnet in Minerals & crystals.

x.d: Red magnesium-aluminium garnet; gem pyrope has been recovered from Colorado and Wyoming.
Violet-red garnet, about two parts pyrope to one part almandine, from Macon County, North Carolina.
Deep red garnet known as carbuncle, the most common gem garnet; name from Alabanda in Asia Minor.
Manganese-aluminium garnet named after Spessart, Bavaria; orange-yellow stones come from Madagascar.
Yellow to cinnamon-brown grossular garnet.
Green grossular garnet from Kenya and Tanzania, first described in the 1960s near Tsavo.
Green andradite garnet, one of the most prized garnets.
Garnet blue-green in daylight and purple or reddish under incandescent light; blue pyrope-spessartine found at Bekily, Madagascar, in the late 1990s.

kinds.d: Loose cut topaz, or topaz cutting rough.

x.d: Yellow, pink-orange or rare pink topaz; Brazilian material can range to deep golden brown, and some stones fade in sunlight.
Naturally blue topaz is rare; colourless or pale stones are heat-treated and irradiated to a deeper blue and sold under shade names.
Colourless topaz with a vapour-deposited coating giving a rainbow surface.

kinds.n: Cut amethyst, citrine and quartz gems
kinds.d: Loose faceted or cabochon quartz gems: amethyst, citrine, ametrine and prasiolite. Uncut amethyst specimens are under Amethyst in Minerals & crystals.

x.d: Violet quartz coloured by iron; sources include Brazil, Uruguay, Zambia and Siberia, where Deep Siberian is the ideal grade.
x.dt: pale lavender to deep purple · colour strongest at tips · fades in light

x.d: Yellow to orange quartz; natural citrine is rare and pale, and most sold is heat-treated amethyst.

v.d: Heated amethyst, deep orange with red flashes

x.d: Quartz with purple and yellow zones; nearly all natural ametrine comes from the Anahí mine in Bolivia.
Green quartz; natural material is rare and most is heat-treated amethyst, notably from the Montezuma mine in Minas Gerais.

kinds.d: Loose opal cut as a cabochon or faceted, or opal rough sold for cutting. Opal specimens and uncut nodules are under Opal in Minerals & crystals.

x.d: Opal with a dark body colour, chiefly from Lightning Ridge, New South Wales; the rarest type.

v.d: From the Royal Peacock mine, Virgin Valley, Nevada

x.d: Opal in thin seams in dark ironstone, from western Queensland (Yowah, Koroit, Jundah, Quilpie).
Light-bodied white opal from Coober Pedy and crystal opal from Mintabie and Andamooka, South Australia.
Transparent to translucent opal with warm yellow to red body colour, chiefly from Querétaro, Mexico.
x.dt: faceted or cabochon · play of colour not required

x.d: Light-bodied opal with vivid play of colour from Wollo Province, found after 2008.
Semi-opaque blue-green opal from Peru with no play of colour, often cut with matrix.

kinds.d: Loose cut olive-green peridot (gem olivine), or peridot cutting rough.

x.d: Peridot from San Carlos, Arizona, now the main source.
Peridot from Zabargad (St John's Island) in the Red Sea, mined from about 300 BCE under the name topazios.
Peridot from the Kaghan Valley, Mansehra District, with silky and rod-like inclusions.
Peridot crystals from pallasite meteorites such as Fukang, Brenham, Esquel, Imilac and Jeppara; lacks nickel unlike terrestrial peridot.

kinds.d: Jadeite and nephrite, carved or cut as cabochons, bangles and beads; graded Type A, B or C by treatment.

x.d: Translucent emerald-green jadeite, the most prized variety; Myanmar's Kachin State supplies over 70% of fine jadeite.
White nephrite from Xinjiang river deposits, prized by Chinese scholars and paid as tribute to the court.
Green nephrite from British Columbia, commercially mined from 1972.
Nephrite from New Zealand's South Island, a protected taonga.

traditions.d: Carving of nephrite and, after about 1800, Burmese jadeite into ceremonial, scholar's and personal objects.
traditions.auth: test for jadeite versus nephrite; Type A/B/C treatment reports for jadeite

notes: Moved out: Ruby in fuchsite and Ruby-zoisite (rocks, belong with Corundum/Zoisite specimens in Minerals). Old Almandine, Demantoid, Hessonite, Pyrope, Rhodolite, Spessartite, Tsavorite, Rubellite, Chrome tourmaline, Imperial/London/Sky/Swiss Blue topaz, Black/Boulder/Fire opal models became archetypes or versions; Grossularite, Malaya garnet and Chocolate opal kept as models (no sourced page found). Gem laboratories are in shelf 01_00. Padparadscha, Kashmir facts from Wikipedia Sapphire page; London/Swiss/Sky shade descriptions are minimal. Lab-grown producers not duplicated here.
